judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: A skip link, 'Skip to navigation', with href="#navigation". In the snapshot, #navigation is the 'News' link, the first item of the primary navigation. The link does just what its text says: it moves to the start of the site navigation. The model mistook the name of the first nav item for where the link goes. The text describes the purpose exactly, so this is not a 2.4.4 failure, and 'Skip to News' would be less accurate.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The 'UK' link (href /uk-news) is one item in the header's News sub-navigation list: World, US politics, UK, Climate crisis, Middle East, Ukraine, and so on, inside the nav landmark. The model had that list and the destination title ('Latest UK news | The Guardian'). On a news site's section bar, 'UK' plainly means the UK news section, just as 'World' means world news, and the link goes there. The purpose can be told from the link text and its nav/list context, so this is no 2.4.4 failure. 'UK news' would be clearer, but that is advice, not a failure.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The 'Learn more' link comes right after the h3 'Deeply read', inside the text 'What readers are spending time with (Learn more)' (snapshot readingText of its container). It goes to 'What is the Deeply read list'. Its purpose follows from the link text with its programmatically determined context: the same sentence/parenthetical and the preceding heading (sufficient technique H80, also G53). The model had both the heading and the surrounding text. It passes 2.4.4 (it would only be an AAA 2.4.9 issue).

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: The element is the Guardian masthead edition picker: a visually hidden checkbox (1x1, clipped, tabindex=-1) used as a CSS toggle, labelled by a visible <label>Int</label>, which opens a list 'International edition / UK edition / US edition / Australia edition / Europe edition'. The live page has the same markup. The finding's wording ('does not say what to enter') and its patch ('Include in masthead') show the model misread it as a data-entry checkbox. Nothing is entered here, and 'Int' does name the current edition. Still, the abbreviation 'Int' does not say that this control switches edition, and a screen reader hears 'Int, checkbox, not checked'. The bigger problem there is the role (4.1.2), not the label's wording. Auditors could reasonably go either way on whether 'Int' is a descriptive enough label for 2.4.6.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: This is the h3 of a Food card, 'Dessert / Henry Harris’ recipe for tarte Vaudoise à la creme'. Neither the h3 nor any ancestor below <html lang="en"> has a lang attribute (the live page is the same), so a screen reader will say the French dish name with English rules. But 3.1.2 exempts proper names, technical terms and phrases that have entered the vernacular. A regional dish name in an English recipe headline ('tarte Vaudoise', capitalised as a name; 'à la crème' close to the naturalised 'à la carte') can be read as a culinary name/term rather than a passage in French. Competent auditors disagree on whether dish names like this need lang markup, so I can't settle it either way.
